title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Landscaping
audience: Landscaping operators, solo or with a team, who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their project size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, project size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a landscaping need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. Write down the landscaping jobs you do well (garden beds, planting plans, paving, and any simple structure you are registered to build), the price range you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each type of client needs the work. Repeat maintenance and planned works on a route you already run often beat one large job across town. Check the registration and insurance limits before you list a service. In Victoria, a registered practitioner is needed when the contract is over $10,000 for domestic building work (Victorian Building Authority, undated).

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. Builders and building practitioners are a referral route for work above the registered-practitioner threshold, according to the VBA's landscaping page. Strata committees decide on major landscaping, which may need a general meeting resolution (Clean Group, 9 March 2026), so a strata manager is a segment with a decision process to plan for. No source was found on property managers or builder referral programmes, so do not add those segments on the strength of this lesson. Record the source and date of each contact, use only business contact details published for business use, and do not buy lists (ACMA, Spam Act obligations, last updated 28 March 2019). Business Queensland advises confirming scope, capacity and deadline before quoting (16 November 2022).

instruction.heading: Watch for public signals
instruction.body: Public planning and building data show where work is being planned and carried out. The Victorian building permit dataset records each permit's location, estimated cost and issue date, and can be filtered by suburb or postcode, but the page read does not show owner or builder names (DataVic, updated 28 August 2026). The City of Casey planning permit register shows projects at application stage, with suburb and status (DataVic, updated 5 November 2026). Each council publishes its own register, so check your own council's. Use this data to choose which suburbs and builders to approach, not to contact an individual home. Public tenders from Buying for Victoria show public projects (7 August 2026).

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A first message to a builder, designer or strata manager names how you learned of the project, makes one verifiable observation (for example, a published tender or public notice whose scope you can meet), and offers one small next step, such as a fifteen-minute call or a written planting scope for a defined area. Keep it short and make it easy to say no. Check consent and unsubscribe rules before any email or text (ACMA). The ACCC's July 2026 review found that many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide the number and timing of follow-ups before the first message. Remove a prospect at once when asked to stop, and record the request and its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced paid work, and move your effort toward them. Silence is not consent.

procedure: Write the job, area, price and project-size criteria for the landscaping work you want, within your registration.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, such as permit registers and tender alerts, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the registration rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A landscaping business covers three suburbs in Melbourne. The Victorian building permit dataset shows a cluster of new house permits in one suburb over the last quarter, and the business is registered for the planting and paving it offers.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner send a sales message to each new home owner, and what should the owner do instead?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner does not message individual home owners using the addresses on the permits. The permit data is used to decide where to market and which builders and building practitioners to approach. The owner contacts builders using contact details published for business use, and checks the Spam Act before any email: ACMA says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The message names the permit activity in general terms, says how the business learned of it, offers a planting scope for a defined area, and asks one question. The owner checks that each service offered is within the registration and insurance held.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, project size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not registered or insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the registration and insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a registered or licensed service in outreach unless you hold the registration or licence that the state where the work is done requires. In Victoria, the VBA sets registered-practitioner and insurance thresholds for domestic building work. In NSW, a licence is needed for structural landscaping over $5,000 including GST (NSW Government, 23 June 2026). This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. ACMA's avoid-spam guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing, a permit register or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7) says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Whether the Act applies to a small business is not confirmed in this lesson.

Telemarketing calls to registered numbers are limited to weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm, and never on Sundays or public holidays (Do Not Call Register industry guide, 2018 copyright notice; check for updates). Wash any call list against the register before calling.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the landscaping work you want, within your registration, before you filter prospects.
Watch public signals, such as permit registers, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned works at a building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the building's manager about the works, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each resident using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the works
Go into the common area to look at the work before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending
